items.title: [Real Estate 101 #8] The Dead Mall Down the Road Is a $70 Million Puzzle — Here's How Developers Solve It
items.body:
> Development deals come in two flavors by *where* they happen — raw land or an already-built site — and one financing engine that decides whether either flavor ever gets out of the ground.

## Today's Concept

When people say "a developer built that," they're compressing three very different jobs into one verb.

**Type 1 — Ground-up on raw or unimproved land.** A farm field at the edge of a growing metro becomes 600 homes, a spine road, sewer lines, and a retail pad. The technical name is *land development* or *master-planned* development. The hard part isn't construction; it's **entitlement** — the legal right to build what you want. Rezoning, site plan approval, traffic studies, environmental review, and a string of public hearings where neighbors show up. Entitlement can take 18 months to five years and can simply fail. The reward for surviving it: land that cost $40,000 an acre as pasture is worth several times that the day the zoning changes, before a single shovel moves.

**Type 2 — Redevelopment of an already-built site.** The dying mall, the vacant office tower, the aging strip center, the 1960s warehouse. Here the land already has infrastructure, roads, and usually decent zoning — which is exactly why the site is expensive. You're buying a building you may not want, so demolition, asbestos abatement, and environmental cleanup enter the budget. Two sub-flavors matter: **teardown-and-rebuild** (raze it, densify it) and **adaptive reuse** (keep the bones, change the use — a warehouse becomes lofts, a mall becomes a town center). Redevelopment also carries a political cost the greenfield deal doesn't: existing tenants, existing neighbors, existing memories.

**Type 3 isn't a place — it's a structure.** This is where most beginners get lost. *Project finance* means the deal is underwritten against the project's own future cash flow and value, not the developer's balance sheet. It's usually held in a single-purpose entity (an LLC that owns exactly one thing), so a failure is walled off from the sponsor's other deals. The money arrives in layers — the **capital stack**:

```
Common equity      (sponsor + investors)  — last paid, highest upside
Preferred / mezz   (11–15% typical)       — fills the gap
Construction loan  (55–65% of cost)       — cheapest, paid first
```

The construction loan is the piece people misunderstand most. You don't get a check at closing. You get a *commitment*, and you draw against it monthly as work is verified — with an interest reserve baked in, because there's no rent yet to pay interest with. It's short (24–36 months), floating-rate, and it must be replaced at the end by a **takeout** (permanent) loan or a sale. That refinancing moment is where a lot of otherwise fine projects died in 2023–2024: costs and rates had moved, and the takeout wouldn't cover the construction loan.

The number that ties all three together is **yield on cost**: stabilized annual net operating income divided by total project cost. Developers compare it to the cap rate that finished buildings trade at. If you build to a 6.5% yield on cost in a market where stabilized assets sell at a 5.25% cap rate, that ~125 basis point spread *is* the development profit. If the spread compresses to zero, the rational move is to buy an existing building instead of building one.

## In Everyday Life

Picture a 1972 enclosed mall on 28 acres in a suburb outside Columbus. Anchor gone, occupancy under 40%, assessed value falling every year — which the city notices, because that's a shrinking tax line.

A developer options the site for $18 million. That's Type 2: redevelopment. The mall's zoning allows retail but not apartments, so step one is entitlement — a rezoning to mixed use, which takes 14 months and three contentious council meetings. Demolition and site prep run $6 million before anything is built.

Total cost pencils at roughly $70 million for 340 apartments plus 40,000 square feet of ground-floor retail. The capital stack: a $42 million construction loan at 60% loan-to-cost drawn monthly, $12 million of preferred equity, $16 million of common equity from the sponsor and a handful of LPs.

The gap is the public infrastructure — new streets, stormwater, a realigned intersection, roughly $9 million of work no lender wants to finance because it produces no rent. So the city creates a **TIF district**: property taxes on the site are frozen at today's depressed level for the taxing bodies, and the *increment* above that — the new taxes generated because the project exists — repays bonds that fund the infrastructure. The city risks future revenue it wouldn't have had otherwise; the developer gets the roads. (This is a real trade-off, not free money: if the increment underperforms, someone is on the hook, and school districts often object because their share is frozen too.)

Three years later, stabilized NOI is $4.6 million on $70 million of cost — a 6.6% yield on cost. Comparable stabilized apartments in that submarket trade near a 5.4% cap rate, implying a value around $85 million. The construction loan is retired with a permanent loan, and the spread between $85 million and $70 million is the return that compensated everyone for four years of risk.

Change one input — construction costs up 12%, or rates up 150 basis points — and that spread vanishes. That's why so many announced projects never break ground.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Development sites come in two kinds: raw land (where entitlement risk dominates) and already-built sites (where acquisition cost, demolition, and politics dominate).
2. Project finance is the engine — a single-purpose entity, a layered capital stack, and a draw-based construction loan that must be replaced by a takeout loan or a sale.
3. The deal only works if yield on cost clears the market cap rate by a meaningful spread; when that spread compresses, building stops even where demand is obvious.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1. (O/X)** A construction loan is funded in full at closing, and the developer holds the cash until it's needed.

**2.** "Entitlement" in development most nearly means:
- (a) Signing the purchase contract for the land
- (b) Securing the legal right to build the use and density you want
- (c) Hiring the general contractor
- (d) Locking the permanent loan rate

**3.** A project underwrites to a 6.5% yield on cost, while similar finished buildings in that market trade at a 5.25% cap rate. This gap primarily represents:
- (a) The developer's compensation for taking construction and lease-up risk
- (b) The interest rate on the construction loan
- (c) The property tax rate
- (d) An error — the two numbers should always match

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Entitlement** — The bundle of government approvals (zoning, site plan, permits) that make a specific project legally buildable on a specific site.
- **Capital stack** — The layered ordering of money in a deal, from senior debt (paid first, lowest return) up to common equity (paid last, highest upside).
- **Loan-to-cost (LTC)** — Construction loan amount divided by total project cost; the lender's measure of how much of the budget it's funding, typically 55–65% in recent years.
- **Yield on cost** — Stabilized net operating income divided by total project cost; compared against market cap rates to judge whether building beats buying.
- **Tax increment financing (TIF)** — A public tool that funds project infrastructure by pledging the *future increase* in property tax revenue the project itself is expected to generate.

---

*Answers: 1 — X (False). Construction loans are drawn in stages as completed work is inspected and verified, which is why an interest reserve is built into the budget. 2 — (b). Entitlement is the legal right to build, and it is usually the single riskiest and least controllable phase of a ground-up deal. 3 — (a). That roughly 125 basis point gap is the development spread: the extra return earned for building an asset rather than buying a finished one. When it compresses toward zero, projects stop penciling.*

items.title: Not the Owner, Just a Tenant: Court Ruling Halts Trump's $400 Million White House Ballroom Plan
items.body:
A federal appeals court has thrown a major legal obstacle in front of one of the Trump administration's most talked-about construction projects: a sprawling, privately funded ballroom addition to the White House estimated at roughly $400 million. In a split 2-1 decision, the panel ordered a halt to further construction until Congress signs off on the plan, setting up what could become a landmark Supreme Court showdown over how much authority a sitting president actually has to remake a building that belongs, in the judges' words, to the nation rather than to any one occupant.

## What the Court Decided

The majority opinion centered on a deceptively simple idea: the president lives in the White House, but does not own it. The building is federal property held in trust for the public, and major structural changes historically have required some form of congressional review or funding approval. The panel found that the ballroom project — one of the largest physical alterations to the executive mansion in decades — crossed a threshold that could not be authorized by executive discretion or private donations alone.

The dissenting judge argued the opposite, warning that the ruling could open the door to years of litigation any time a future president wants to renovate, redecorate, or expand facilities at the White House, and that courts should be cautious about inserting themselves into decisions traditionally left to the executive branch.

## The Project at the Center of the Fight

The ballroom itself has been pitched by supporters as a long-overdue upgrade, giving the White House a modern, large-capacity event space for state dinners and diplomatic functions instead of relying on tents erected on the South Lawn. Backers point out that the project is being funded largely through private donations rather than taxpayer dollars, arguing that this should insulate it from the kind of congressional budget scrutiny that applies to publicly financed construction.

Critics counter that the source of funding is beside the point. Because the White House is a historic landmark and a symbol of the presidency itself, they argue any project of this scale — reshaping sightlines, altering historic structures, and potentially affecting the building's protected architectural character — needs sign-off from bodies like the National Capital Planning Commission and, ultimately, lawmakers who oversee federal property.

## Why This Case Matters Beyond the Ballroom

Legal analysts following the case say the real stakes go well past a single construction project. At issue is a broader question: where does presidential discretion over the White House end, and where does congressional and public oversight begin? Past presidents have made changes to the residence — from added balconies to renovated offices — but few, if any, have approached this scale or price tag, which is part of why the case has drawn attention from constitutional scholars as well as historic preservation advocates.

A ruling that stands would reinforce the idea that the White House functions similarly to other protected federal landmarks, where alterations are subject to institutional checks regardless of who currently occupies the building. A reversal, on the other hand, would give future presidents considerably more latitude to fund and execute large-scale changes using private money, sidestepping the usual congressional appropriations process.

## What Happens Next

The administration is expected to appeal, and most observers believe the dispute is likely headed toward the Supreme Court given the constitutional questions involved about separation of powers and control over the "people's house." Construction crews have reportedly paused major work on the site while the legal process plays out, though preliminary planning and design work may continue.

For now, the ruling stands as a reminder that even the president's own residence comes with limits — a reminder rooted less in politics than in a basic legal principle: occupancy is not the same as ownership.

items.title: A 4 A.M. Vote, a 50-49 Margin: How Trump's Former Lawyer Became America's Attorney General
items.body:
## A Senate Floor Nearly Empty, a Nation Watching

Just before dawn, in a chamber thinned out by exhaustion and long past the hour most Americans had gone to sleep, the U.S. Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as the next attorney general of the United States. The final tally — 50 to 49 — was as narrow as confirmation votes get, and it capped weeks of stop-and-start negotiations that had, at several points, looked like they might end in defeat for the nomination.

Blanche's path to the country's top law enforcement post was unusual by any measure. Before his nomination, he was best known as one of Donald Trump's personal defense attorneys, representing the former and now-sitting president in a series of high-profile legal battles. That history was always going to shape how the confirmation fight unfolded, and it did — turning what might otherwise have been a routine cabinet vote into a referendum on the independence of the Justice Department itself.

## A Long, Uneven Road to Confirmation

Support for the nomination did not move in a straight line. Momentum stalled repeatedly in committee and on the floor, as senators from both parties raised questions about how a nominee with such close personal and professional ties to the president would navigate the traditional wall between the White House and federal law enforcement. Two Republican senators ultimately broke with their party to vote against confirmation, a defection significant enough that it left leadership with almost no margin for additional losses.

Those defections, according to aides familiar with the closed-door talks, centered less on Blanche's legal credentials — which supporters describe as substantial — and more on broader concerns about precedent: what it means for an attorney general to arrive at the job directly from representing the president in his own legal proceedings. Democrats were unanimous in opposition, framing the nomination as emblematic of a broader effort to align the Justice Department more closely with the White House's political interests.

## Why the Vote Happened at 4 A.M.

The overnight timing was not incidental. Senate leadership scheduled the final vote for the early morning hours after a lengthy series of procedural motions and extended floor speeches from opponents, who used the available time to press their objections on the record. Supporters of the nomination argued the delay tactics were more about signaling than substance, since the outcome had been effectively locked in once vote-counters secured a bare majority earlier in the week. Critics countered that the extraordinary hour underscored just how contested the process had become.

Whatever the intent, the image of a wafer-thin majority pushing through a confirmation vote while most of the country slept has become its own story — a visual shorthand for a nomination that never enjoyed broad, comfortable support.

## What Comes Next for the Justice Department

Blanche now inherits a department facing no shortage of institutional pressure, including ongoing questions about prosecutorial independence, staffing turnover, and how the office manages politically sensitive cases involving the administration itself. Legal analysts across the ideological spectrum have said the new attorney general's early decisions — particularly any involving matters connected to the president he once represented — will be closely watched as an early test of how he intends to draw, or not draw, boundaries between his past role and his new one.

Former Justice Department officials, speaking generally about the transition rather than about Blanche specifically, have noted that attorneys general who arrive with strong personal loyalties to a president often face a defining moment early in their tenure when those loyalties and the department's institutional obligations appear to pull in different directions. How that moment is handled, they say, tends to shape the rest of a tenure.

## A Divided Chamber, A Divided Reaction

Reaction on Capitol Hill broke along familiar lines. Supporters of the confirmation pointed to Blanche's trial experience and argued that personal association with a president is not, on its own, disqualifying — noting that past attorneys general have also had prior political or personal ties to the administrations they served. Opponents maintained that the closeness of this particular relationship, combined with the unusually narrow vote, leaves the department starting its next chapter under a cloud of skepticism it did not choose and cannot easily dispel.

For now, the numbers speak for themselves: a single vote, cast in the small hours of the morning, was enough to install Todd Blanche as the nation's chief law enforcement officer — and enough to leave Washington debating what that margin says about the office he now leads.

items.title: The Moratorium Ticket: Why 2026 Governor's Races Are Turning Into Referendums on Data Centers
items.body:
## A New Kind of Campaign Issue

Data centers used to be the kind of infrastructure story that stayed in trade publications and local zoning meetings. Heading into the 2026 midterms, that has changed. In statehouse races from the upper Midwest to the Gulf Coast, candidates are discovering that a pledge to pause, slow, or tightly regulate new data center construction can be as galvanizing on the campaign trail as taxes or crime once were.

The shift reflects a simple reality: the artificial intelligence boom has a physical footprint, and voters are starting to feel it in ways that show up on monthly bills rather than in abstract debates about technology policy.

## Power Bills Are the Trigger

The core grievance driving this trend is economic, not ideological. Data centers, particularly the large campuses built to train and run AI models, consume enormous amounts of electricity — often as much as a mid-sized city. In several states, utilities have proposed or won approval for new transmission lines, gas plants, and rate structures tied directly to serving these facilities.

Ratepayer advocates and some state regulators have raised concerns that the cost of that new capacity is, in part, being spread across residential customers rather than falling solely on the companies building the data centers. That dynamic has given candidates a tangible, kitchen-table argument: household electricity bills rising while nearby land is cleared for server farms that employ relatively few permanent workers once construction ends.

Water use has become a parallel flashpoint, particularly in warmer or drought-prone regions, where cooling systems for large facilities draw on municipal or groundwater supplies that communities also rely on for drinking water and agriculture.

## A Rare Point of Bipartisan Overlap

What makes this cycle notable is that the skepticism doesn't sort neatly along party lines. In traditionally conservative areas, opposition has often centered on local control, property rights, and protecting agricultural land and rural water tables from industrial-scale development. In more liberal areas, the emphasis tends to fall on environmental review, corporate accountability for infrastructure costs, and equitable rate-setting.

The result, in states like Wisconsin, Ohio, and Florida, is a political environment where gubernatorial hopefuls from both parties have found room to campaign on similar-sounding promises — tighter permitting, mandatory community benefit agreements, or outright moratoriums on new approvals pending further study — even if their underlying rationale and preferred policy fixes diverge once the specifics are debated.

## The Industry's Counterargument

Technology companies and utility groups have pushed back, arguing that data centers bring significant tax revenue, construction jobs, and long-term investment to host communities, and that they are frequently required to fund the very grid upgrades critics say burden ratepayers. Industry representatives also note that many new facilities are contracting directly for renewable power or paying premiums specifically to avoid shifting costs onto residential customers.

State economic development officials in several of these races have warned that a blanket moratorium risks pushing investment — and the jobs and tax base that come with it — to more permissive states or countries, without necessarily solving the underlying grid capacity questions that predate the AI boom.

## What to Watch Before November

For voters trying to sort rhetoric from policy, a few questions are worth tracking as these races develop:

- **Who pays for grid upgrades?** Watch for specific proposals on cost allocation between large industrial customers and residential ratepayers, since this is the mechanism most directly tied to bill increases.
- **What counts as a "pause"?** Moratorium proposals vary widely — some target new permit approvals only, others would halt projects already under construction, which raises separate legal and contractual questions.
- **How is water use measured and disclosed?** Facilities using air-cooling versus water-cooling systems have very different local impacts, and state-level transparency requirements differ significantly.

As with most infrastructure fights that reach the ballot box, the details of implementation are likely to matter more than the campaign slogans. Whether "the moratorium ticket" becomes a durable governing agenda or a rhetorical high point of the 2026 cycle will depend largely on how these candidates translate a popular grievance into workable regulation once they're in office.

*This article summarizes publicly reported trends in state-level campaigns and is intended for general informational purposes. Readers should consult local election coverage and candidate platforms for specifics in their state.*
